structure.title: Ideas and inference
structure.text: Early sections distinguish mental contents and examine how people reason beyond what is immediately present.

structure.title: Consequences of the inquiry
structure.text: Later sections apply the analysis to necessity, freedom, miracles, religion, and the limits of scepticism.

people.name: Impression
people.text: Hume's word for the lively, immediate perceptions we have when we see, hear or feel something, which he takes as the source of all our thinking.

people.name: Idea
people.text: A fainter copy of an impression, recalled or combined by the mind; Hume asks which impression any idea comes from, and rejects ideas with none.

people.name: Custom
people.text: The habit by which, having seen one thing follow another again and again, we expect it to happen next time; Hume argues reason cannot justify it.

context.title: Experience and proof
context.text: Hume distinguishes demonstrative reasoning from expectations about matters of fact. Strong confidence does not automatically supply a logical guarantee.
context.takeaway: Ask what kind of support a claim has.

context.title: Scepticism in ordinary life
context.text: The argument challenges philosophical justifications while acknowledging that people continue forming expectations and acting. Doubt has practical limits.
context.takeaway: Distinguish explaining belief from eliminating it.

notice.text: Follow the move from repeated events to necessity.
notice.why: It identifies the inference Hume wants explained.
Reports require comparison with other experience.

opening: The sun has risen every morning you remember. That gives you confidence it will rise tomorrow, but Hume asks what justifies the step from what has happened to what must happen next. The answer proves harder than ordinary life allows us to notice. His investigation follows the difficulty into cause and effect, freedom, and reports of miracles. Calm, lucid sentences uncover how much of our reasoning rests on habits we cannot establish by the kind of proof we thought we possessed.
